description: We are Satellar 4, creators of Stellar Variability Explorer, an interactive platform powered by real NASA SPHEREx data. Our mission is to make astronomy accessible to everyone through interactive sky exploration, temporal and spectral analysis, and scientific resources. Supporting seven languages, five educational levels, and 770 scientific explanations. We believe everyone deserves the opportunity to explore the universe!rse!
summary: Stellar Variability Explorer is Satellar 4's web application for exploring NASA SPHEREx infrared observations and understanding their scientific limitations. It brings together an interactive sky atlas, prepared observations of five celestial targets, image comparison, and a dedicated RW Aurigae spectral laboratory. WISE/unWISE imagery and Gaia catalogue references provide complementary context. A rule-based Scientific Reliability Assistant explains uncertainties, quality flags, saturation, and differences in wavelength that can affect interpretation. Multilingual educational content offers adjustable learning levels to make astronomical evidence more accessible. The project addresses the challenge of helping the public explore sky images and compare observations over time, while separating apparent differences from established physical changes. It supports learning and preliminary investigation; it does not establish a new discovery or confirmed motion or variability.
details:
Problem and connection to the challenge

Astronomical archives contain observations that can be difficult to access, compare, and interpret without specialist tools. Stellar Variability Explorer brings SPHEREx imagery, prepared observations, spectral records, and educational explanations into a web application. Its public-facing sky exploration and temporal comparison workflows address the aims of Planet X and SPHEREx: helping people explore infrared sky images and investigate how observations differ over time. An image difference is a starting point for investigation, rather than sufficient evidence of an astrophysical change.

Current capabilities documented in the project report

The Interactive Sky Atlas uses Aladin Lite and NASA/IPAC IRSA's SPHEREx DR1 HiPS service. It supports sky navigation, object-name searches, RA/Dec coordinate entry, field-of-view controls, spectral-channel browsing, coordinate grids, and links that preserve selected viewing parameters. The all-sky atlas provides spectral exploration; changing a spectral channel does not represent changing the observation date.

The prepared observational collection comprises 28 SPHEREx frames across Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis. Nine are longer-wavelength D6 frames. Sky Explorer presents blink animation, side-by-side and slider comparisons, observation dates, effective wavelengths, detector information, quality masks, and catalogue position references. The preparation workflow uses FITS metadata, World Coordinate System transformations, image alignment, and quality assessment. These are prepared observations of selected targets, not a completed service for retrieving time-series imagery at arbitrary coordinates.

The RW Aurigae laboratory presents 279 spectral measurement records across five SPHEREx detector arrays. Its views include flux distributions, uncertainties, observation timelines, time-wavelength coverage, quality flags, and individual records. These records support inspection of the available measurements; they do not by themselves establish intrinsic variability.

Multi-mission exploration combines SPHEREx and historical WISE/unWISE imagery with WiseView sequences and Gaia DR3 astrometric references. The report describes SPHEREx/unWISE comparisons for all five prepared targets and Gaia references for three catalogue sources. Different missions provide complementary information, but their images are not automatically equivalent in wavelength, angular resolution, calibration, or observation epoch.

The Scientific Reliability Assistant provides transparent, rule-based explanations of measurement uncertainty, signal-to-noise limitations, saturation, missing data, detector differences, effective wavelengths, and quality flags. It is not an independently trained AI prediction model or a validated discovery classifier.

The Learning Studio offers 25 concepts across five learning levels and seven languages: English, Persian, Arabic, French, Spanish, Simplified Chinese, and Russian. Age group and explanation complexity can be selected independently. The resulting 875 concept-language-level combinations describe the content structure, rather than a measured educational outcome. The media library is documented as 12 entries, including eight local MP4 files. Materials include NASA SPHEREx animations, WiseView examples, and Canadian Space Agency NEOSSat imagery of Comet C/2020 F3 NEOWISE.

Tools and access

The documented technology stack uses React, TypeScript, and Vite for the interface; Python, Astropy, NumPy, and SciPy for data preparation; and Aladin Lite for sky visualization. FITS, WCS, and HiPS connect the data preparation and visualization workflows. The supplied project address is hosted on Cloudflare Pages.

The report describes online and standalone offline editions. The offline edition is intended to provide prepared images, spectral records, educational content, and local media. Live sky imagery and external archive services require internet access. A downloadable offline package was not supplied with this submission material.

Creativity, benefits, and intended use

The project's creative contribution is the combination of sky exploration, prepared temporal comparisons, spectral inspection, explicit interpretation limits, and multilingual learning in one interface. Students, educators, astronomy enthusiasts, and citizen scientists can use it to investigate observations and ask better questions about evidence. Its intended benefit is easier access to astronomical data and scientific reasoning; improved learning or discovery performance has not been measured here.

Limitations

Saturation, missing values, quality flags, wavelength differences, and astrometric limitations constrain interpretation of the prepared observations. The supplied report does not establish a confident detection of WISE 0855 or confirmed physical motion or intrinsic brightness changes in the prepared targets. Differences between instruments or channels must not be presented as proof of temporal change. The identity of one historical recording associated with R Draconis remains unverified and should not be treated as a confirmed observation of that target.

Automated retrieval and processing of multi-epoch FITS observations at arbitrary coordinates remains incomplete; the report describes browser access limitations and an external IRSA search pathway. All-sky navigation does not remove this limitation. The reported software tests are not evidence of a validated astronomical discovery or measured educational effectiveness.

Future development

Planned work includes more automated archive retrieval, better wavelength-matched comparisons, additional verified measurements, and more quantitative analysis. These are future directions, not completed capabilities.

AI assistance

ChatGPT and Codex supported research, software development, debugging, educational content, testing work, and documentation. Claude and ChatGPT also assisted with the team logo and media work; Claude is specifically credited with audio-enhancement assistance, and Adobe Premiere Pro was used for editing. The Scientific Reliability Assistant itself is rule-based. The astronomical observations and measurement records are attributed to the scientific sources listed below, not to generative AI.
